Build a useful shopping list: vegetables, fruit, tofu, beans, oats, eggs, plain dairy, fish and nuts. Start with what you can find and enjoy locally.
Studies or official product pages linked
Skip the hunt for a miracle food. Choose a few things you can eat often, at prices and portions that fit your life.

A means strong guidance or consistent research. B means useful research exists, but your own result remains uncertain. C means evidence comes mainly from related activities, with little direct evidence. Each letter applies to the claim on that card.
Build the base of everyday meals
Seasonal produce, beans and whole grains are ordinary groceries. Choose a mix that fits local prices and your tastes.
Start with seasonal vegetables and whole fruit, and add some vegetables to each meal. Frozen vegetables can fill the gap when fresh preparation is difficult.
WHO recommends at least 400 g of vegetables and fruit per day for people over ten. Chinese dietary guidance also calls for daily produce.
Juice does not fully replace whole fruit. Adjust for local prices, taste and digestion.
Keep a bag of plain frozen vegetables for steaming, boiling or stir-frying. For canned vegetables, look for lower-sodium options.
WHO says frozen and canned produce can be healthy choices when they have no added sugar or excess sodium.
Check breading, sauces and sodium. Compare prices per edible serving rather than per package.
Rotate tofu, dried beans and lower-sodium canned beans. Add them to soups, rice or stir-fries for a plant protein option.
WHO recommends pulses; the Chinese dietary guidelines also recommend soy foods.
Avoid beans if you are allergic. If they cause bloating, start small; check sodium in seasoned tofu and canned beans.
Replace part of your white rice with oats, brown rice or mixed grains. Check the ingredients on oats; plain versions make added sugar easier to control.
WHO recommends that carbohydrates come mainly from whole grains, produce and pulses. Chinese guidelines also encourage whole grains.
You do not need to switch everything at once. Start small if your digestion is sensitive, and buy only what you can use.
Eggs, dairy, fish and nuts each have a place. Rotating them helps you eat a wider range of foods.
Boil, steam or lightly fry an egg, then add vegetables and a staple grain for an easy meal.
Chinese dietary guidelines recommend eggs in moderation and say there is no need to discard the yolk.
Eggs cannot provide all your protein variety. Avoid them if you are allergic.
American Heart Association · Protein and heart health
Choose plain milk or unsweetened yogurt for breakfast or a snack. Compare prices per 100 ml or grams and check for added sugar.
Chinese dietary guidelines identify dairy as part of a balanced diet and recommend a variety of dairy foods.
If you cannot tolerate lactose or are allergic to dairy, choose an option that suits you. Check sugar in flavored yogurt.
Everyday fish, frozen fish and canned sardines
When the price works, choose ordinary fresh or frozen fish or canned sardines and serve them with vegetables. Expensive fish are not required.
The American Heart Association recommends two fish servings a week, particularly fatty fish. The FDA counts canned, frozen and fresh fish as options.
Check sodium in canned fish. During pregnancy or breastfeeding, and for children, follow advice on mercury levels by species.
American Heart Association · Fish and omega-3 (2024)
Swap a sugary snack for a small handful of plain peanuts or other nuts. A large bag saves money only if you will eat it.
WHO includes nuts in a healthy diet; Chinese guidelines recommend them in moderation.
Nuts are energy dense, so keep portions modest. Avoid peanuts or tree nuts if you are allergic.
The oil you cook with, a little less salt and one fewer sugary drink are practical places to start.
Cook with common oils such as canola or soybean oil in place of some butter or lard, while keeping an eye on the total amount.
WHO recommends replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat and lists soybean and canola oils as options.
There is no need to buy an expensive oil. A different oil is not a reason to use more of it.
Swap one sweet drink for water
Start with the sweet drink you have most often and try water or unsweetened tea instead.
WHO recommends limiting free sugars, including those in fruit juice.
Follow medical fluid restrictions if you have them. You need not change every drink overnight.
Use a little less salt and sauce
Use slightly less salt or salty sauce when cooking. Compare sodium levels on packaged foods.
WHO advises adults to keep salt below 5 g per day. Less sodium can help lower blood pressure.
If you have kidney disease or special treatment, ask a clinician before switching to a low-sodium salt.
After trying it, vote to tell other readers whether you would recommend it.
Adjust for allergies, illness or special nutrition needs with qualified advice. No single food makes a whole diet healthy.
